Conjugates of platinum nanoparticles with gallium tetra – (4-Carboxyphenyl) porphyrin and their use in photodynamic antimicrobial chemotherapy when in solution or embedded in electrospun fiber

Department of Chemistry, Rhodes University, Grahamstown 6140, South Africa

Photodynamic antimicrobial chemotherapy
A B S T R A C T
The conjugation of Pt nanoparticles with ClGa(III) 5,10,15,20-tetrakis-(4-carboxyphenyl) porphyrin (ClGaTCPP) showed greater antimicrobial activity against a gram positive and drug resistant bacteria Staphylococcus aureus, than when the porphyrin was used alone. ClGaTCPP and its conjugate with platinum nanoparticle was successfully electrospun into a polystyrene polymer where the diameter ranged from 10 to $22\mu \mathrm{m}$ . The conjugates within the fiber still showed activity towards S. aureus.

1. Introduction
Metal nanoparticles (NPs) have become of great interest in research as they find applications in different fields such as electrochemistry, catalysis and biology $[1]$ . Biological applications of metal NPs include as photosensitizers in photodynamic therapy (PDT) of cancer and in drug delivery $[2]$ . Metal NPs (such as Ag or Pt) have also been reported to have antibacterial and antifungal properties $[3]$ . Metal NPs attach to the cell wall of the fungi or bacteria through self-assembly due to their small size, causing cell death $[4,5]$ .

To understand why this research is significant, we must first look at the unique properties of metal nanoparticles. In the realm of nanotechnology, "nanoparticles" refers to particles with at least one dimension between 1 and 100 nanometers. At this scale, materials exhibit behaviors that are distinct from their bulk counterparts. For instance, in biology, metal NPs are not just passive carriers; they are active agents. They can act as **photosensitizers** in **photodynamic therapy (PDT)**, a treatment for cancer where light activates a chemical to destroy tumor cells.
